title: Rank the guesses
briefing: Before the attacker got in as svc_backup, `var/log/secure` filled with failed SSH passwords from 203.0.113.66. A brute force has a shape: which accounts it hammered tells you which wordlist it used and what else on your estate is exposed.
Rank the usernames the attacker tried. The ranking is the deliverable, not a feeling about it.

lesson.p: `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` is the most-used pipeline in log triage: sort so identical lines sit together, count each run, then sort the counts biggest first. `head` turns it into a top-N.

flags: sort lines as text, byte by byte under LC_ALL=C
numeric order / reverse order. `-nr` is biggest first.
sort and drop duplicate lines in one step
split on commas and sort numerically on field 2 only. `-k2` without `,2` means from field 2 to the END of the line.
collapse ADJACENT identical lines into one; that is why input is sorted first
prefix each line with how many times it repeated
print only lines that repeat / only lines that appear once
keep the first N lines: the top N after `sort -nr`

lesson.note: `uniq` only compares a line with the one before it. Unsorted input gives wrong counts and no error: `a b a` counts as three different lines.

Locale changes sort order. This VM runs with `LC_ALL=C`, which sorts by byte value: `A B a b`. A RHEL host defaults to `en_US.UTF-8`, which sorts `a A b B` and gives punctuation a lower weight, so the same file can sort differently on a colleague's shell, and tools that need sorted input (`uniq`, `comm`, `join`) quietly misbehave when the two sides were sorted under different locales. In scripts, set `LC_ALL=C` before sorting.

stages.why: Puts identical IPs next to each other so uniq can see them.
One line per IP, prefixed with its count.
Numeric, reversed: the noisiest client on top. Here it is the scanner, 203.0.113.9.
Field 10 is the response size in bytes.
Drop `-`, which Apache writes when no body was sent. `--` ends grep's options, so the pattern `-` is not read as a flag.
Sorted as text: 1840 comes before 196 because the character 8 sorts before 9, and 87 lands last.
`-n` compares whole numbers, `-u` keeps one of each. Now 87 is first and 5312 last.
Fields are separated by a single space.
Sort key is field 2 only, compared as a number. Without a key, sort would order by user name.
Merge both lists in sorted order; a name in both files now appears twice in a row.
Print only the lines that repeat: the overlap. `uniq -u` would print the names on exactly one team.

challenge.question: Counting only the Failed password lines in var/log/secure that come from 203.0.113.66, which username did the attacker try most often, and how many times?
challenge.format: The count, one space, then the username, the way uniq -c prints it, for example 12 admin

hints: Keep only the attacker's failed passwords, isolate the username on each line, then count. Some lines say `for invalid user NAME from`, others `for NAME from`: the name is always the word just before ` from 203.0.113.66`.
`grep -oE '[^ ]+ from 203\.0\.113\.66 '` prints the username plus the rest of the match; `cut -d' ' -f1` keeps the name. Then `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -1`.
grep 'Failed password' var/log/secure | grep -oE '[^ ]+ from 203\.0\.113\.66 ' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -___ | head -1

debrief.solution: grep 'Failed password' var/log/secure | grep -oE '[^ ]+ from 203\.0\.113\.66 ' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -1
debrief.alternative: grep -F 'from 203.0.113.66 ' var/log/secure | grep 'Failed password' | grep -oE '[a-z_]+ from' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | head -n1
why: The top guess, ftpuser, was never going to work. svc_backup, the account that fell, got only 5 attempts. The ranking shows the wordlist, not the weak spot. Check that every guessed name either does not exist or has key-only SSH, then look at why svc_backup accepted a password at all.

On RHEL the fixes are in sshd's own configuration and in PAM: `PasswordAuthentication no` in a drop-in under `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` (confirm the effective value with `sshd -T`), and `pam_faillock` to lock an account after repeated failures, which the RHEL STIG requires.
Before you trust `sort -nr | head -1`, check for ties: run it with `head -3`. postgres and jenkins tie at 7, one behind ftpuser at 8. If the top two were tied, `head -1` would silently pick one.
